It addresses the inefficiency of fixed-step ray marching in sparse environments by dynamically allocating memory based on actual occupancy [S1, unofficial].

The evidence describes a two-pass CUDA kernel approach where the first pass counts traversal steps to determine the exact number of samples needed, and the second pass fills pre-allocated buffers with these samples. This mechanism directly addresses the inefficiency of fixed-step ray marching (which would allocate memory for the maximum possible steps regardless of actual occupancy) by dynamically allocating memory based on the actual number of traversal steps (occupancy) per ray.
